articles.hook: Trong thông cáo gửi tới hãng tin Reuters, Dreame gọi đây là một "lựa chọn chiến lược chủ động" sau khi đánh giá lại chu kỳ nghiên cứu - phát triển (R&D), quy trình sản xuất của ngành ô tô, áp lực cạnh tranh thị trường cũng như cường độ vốn đầu tư cần duy trì.

sections.heading: Điều gì đã xảy ra
sections.body: Trong thông cáo gửi tới hãng tin Reuters, Dreame gọi đây là một "lựa chọn chiến lược chủ động" sau khi đánh giá lại chu kỳ nghiên cứu - phát triển (R&D), quy trình sản xuất của ngành ô tô, áp lực cạnh tranh thị trường cũng như cường độ vốn đầu tư cần duy trì.

sections.heading: Các nguồn đang khớp nhau ở đâu
sections.body: Quyết định dừng kế hoạch thương mại hóa phương tiện độc lập kéo theo sự thay đổi lớn về cơ cấu tổ chức của Dreame . Tờ Economic Daily đưa tin, đội ngũ nhân sự tham gia dự án xe điện của Dreame từng đạt quy mô cao điểm gần 1. 000 người vào cuối năm 2025 thì nay thu hẹp xuống còn vài chục nhân viên. Nhóm người vẫn công tác còn lại chủ yếu thuộc bộ phận tài chính, pháp chế và nhân sự, chịu trách nhiệm xử lý những công việc tồn đọng như quyết toán công nợ với các nhà cung ứng và thực hiện thủ tục giải thể doanh nghiệp.

sections.heading: Dữ kiện hiện có
sections.body: Theo trang tin tài chính Yicai (Trung Quốc), nhiều nhân sự quản lý cấp cao của dự án đã bắt đầu tìm kiếm cơ hội việc làm mới. Các đợt cắt giảm nhân sự và từ chức liên tiếp diễn ra từ tháng 5. 2026 đã khiến phần lớn diện tích văn phòng làm việc của dự án rơi vào tình trạng bỏ trống. Nguồn tin từ tờ China Economic Net dẫn lời một số cựu nhân viên cho biết ngân sách phát triển của dự án trước đây phụ thuộc một phần vào việc tìm kiếm các nhà đầu tư bên ngoài hoặc khoản trợ cấp. Tuy nhiên, những nội dung này chưa được Dreame xác nhận chính thức.

sections.heading: Ai nên chú ý lúc này
sections.body: Dự án xe điện được Dreame công bố từ tháng 8. 2025, với mục tiêu ứng dụng thế mạnh về động cơ tốc độ cao của hãng vào phương tiện di chuyển thông minh và chế tạo mẫu xe có tốc độ hàng đầu thế giới. Để phục vụ mục tiêu này, Dreame từng công bố kế hoạch mở chuỗi showroom tại khu vực Trung Đông (gồm Iraq, Ả Rập Xê Út, UAE, Qatar) và chi 10 triệu USD cho đoạn phim quảng cáo 30 giây tại giải bóng bầu dục Super Bowl (Mỹ) vào tháng 2. 2026.

sections.heading: Điều chưa rõ
sections.body: Tại triển lãm CES 2026 và sự kiện giới thiệu ở San Francisco (Mỹ) vào tháng 4, Dreame trưng bày xe mẫu Nebula NEXT 01 phiên bản JET Edition. Theo công bố của hãng tại thời điểm đó, xe được thiết kế với 4 hệ dẫn động điện cùng 2 động cơ phản lực nhiên liệu rắn, cung cấp lực đẩy 100 kN và có khả năng tăng tốc 0 - 100 km/giờ trong 0,9 giây. Hãng cũng thông báo thử nghiệm thành công trong phòng thí nghiệm mẫu cell pin thể rắn gốc sunfua 60 Ah với mật độ năng lượng trên 450 Wh/kg.

Tuy nhiên, theo China Economic Net , các cựu nhân viên xác nhận phương tiện xuất hiện tại triển lãm chủ yếu mang tính chất trình diễn, phục vụ truyền thông. Mẫu xe tại CES chưa có khung gầm hoàn chỉnh và phải điều khiển từ xa, còn phương tiện trưng bày tại San Francisco được phát triển dựa trên khung vỏ có sẵn. Các báo cáo phân tích công nghệ cũng lưu ý thông số pin thể rắn và khả năng tăng tốc 0,9 giây của xe chưa đi kèm các dữ liệu đo kiểm độc lập được công bố rộng rãi.

articles.title: Đánh giá Sony Bravia 5: Khi công nghệ Mini-LED cao cấp trở nên dễ tiếp cận hơn
articles.hook: Liệu một chiếc TV 'giá mềm' của Sony có thể thách thức các đối thủ giá rẻ từ Trung Quốc bằng chất lượng hình ảnh chuẩn điện ảnh?
articles.summary: Sony Bravia 5 đánh dấu bước chuyển mình của hãng trong phân khúc TV tầm trung với tấm nền Mini-LED Master Backlight Drive, mang lại độ tương phản ấn tượng và hiệu suất chơi game 120Hz mượt mà.
articles.dek: Dòng TV mới của Sony xóa nhòa khoảng cách với các model cao cấp nhờ bộ xử lý XR và hệ thống làm mờ cục bộ 240 vùng, dù vẫn còn một số hạn chế về cổng kết nối và độ sáng so với dòng Bravia 7.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: Trong lịch sử, Sony thường gặp khó khăn trong việc duy trì tiêu chuẩn cao cấp trên các dòng TV phổ thông. Tuy nhiên, Bravia 5 (mã hiệu K65XR55 cho bản 65 inch) đã thay đổi định kiến này. Được định vị là dòng TV Mini-LED giá cả phải chăng nhất của hãng trong năm 2025, sản phẩm này kế thừa nhiều đặc tính kỹ thuật từ các dòng cao cấp để cạnh tranh trực tiếp trong thị trường TV 4K đang ngày càng khốc liệt.

sections.heading: Thay đổi kỹ thuật: Sức mạnh từ Master Backlight Drive và chip XR
sections.body: Thay đổi cốt lõi nằm ở việc trang bị tấm nền VA Mini-LED với hệ thống điều khiển Master Backlight Drive, hỗ trợ làm mờ cục bộ (local dimming) trên khoảng 240 vùng độc lập. TV duy trì tần số quét thực 120Hz và được vận hành bởi bộ xử lý hình ảnh XR danh tiếng. Về âm thanh, hệ thống loa 40W Acoustic Multi-Audio bao gồm hai loa toàn dải và hai loa tweeter khung (frame tweeter) hỗ trợ cả Dolby Atmos và DTS:X.

sections.heading: The evidence so far
sections.body: Trong thử nghiệm thực tế, Bravia 5 đạt độ sáng tối đa gần 900 nits (cửa sổ 10% HDR) và duy trì 595 nits trên toàn màn hình, vượt qua nhiều đối thủ OLED. Hình ảnh có độ tương phản sâu, hiện tượng hở sáng (blooming) được kiểm soát tốt. Đặc biệt, tính năng 'Perfect For PlayStation 5' giúp tự động tối ưu hóa HDR khi kết nối với máy game PS5, kết hợp với độ trễ đầu vào thấp chỉ 13. 3ms ở 60Hz mang lại trải nghiệm giải trí mượt mà.

sections.heading: Giới hạn và rủi ro: Sự đánh đổi về kết nối và độ sáng
sections.body: Để có mức giá cạnh tranh, Bravia 5 bị cắt giảm số vùng làm mờ và độ sáng so với Bravia 7. Một hạn chế đáng tiếc là chỉ có 2 trong số 4 cổng HDMI hỗ trợ đầy đủ tính năng 2. 1 (4K/120Hz, VRR). Ngoài ra, góc nhìn của tấm nền VA còn hạn chế khi hiện tượng hở sáng dễ lộ diện nếu xem từ góc lệch. Sony cũng tiếp tục nói không với định dạng HDR10+ và không có chế độ Filmmaker Mode chuyên dụng.

sections.heading: What is still unclear
sections.body: Dù có giá từ 1. 399 USD cho bản 55 inch, Bravia 5 vẫn cao hơn đáng kể so với các đối thủ như TCL C7K. Người dùng cần theo dõi các chương trình khuyến mãi để có mức giá tốt hơn. Ngoài ra, việc tích hợp sâu hệ sinh thái Google TV và các dịch vụ độc quyền như Sony Pictures Core (tặng 10 phim và 24 tháng streaming) sẽ là yếu tố then chốt để người dùng quyết định chi thêm tiền cho thương hiệu Nhật Bản thay vì các lựa chọn giá rẻ.

draft_context.source_title: I tested Sony’s affordable Bravia 5 TV, and it offers a lot of punch for its price tag, throwing serious shade on Sony’s previous mid-range screens
draft_context.description: Sony Bravia 5: Two-minute review The Sony Bravia 5 is a mini-LED TV with crisp images, strong contrast and great gaming features. It occupies that level in Sony’s TV range where the brand has historically struggled to maintain its high standards. The Bravia 5, though, bucks this trend in pretty spectacular fashion. The Sony Bravia 5 retains both mini-LED lighting and local dimming, for starters, as well as an 120Hz panel to keep gamers happy. Sony says the Bravia 5 LCD panels are still made to the brand’s Master Backlight Drive standard too, and they’re equipped with a full up-to-date version of the Google TV smart system. There are ‘catches’ to this promising specification, of course. In particular, the Bravia 5 won’t benefit from as many dimming zones as the step up Bravia 7, or achieve so much brightness. In reality, though, the 65-inch Bravia 5 (AKA the K65XR55) delivers much less of a step down from Sony’s mid-range models than expected based on past Sony lines. Pictures are vibrant, crisp, full of contrast and just way less compromised than previous generations of the same level of Sony TV would have been. Add punchy, clean and detailed audio to its surprising picture talents, and the Bravia 5 is the Sony value TV we’ve always wanted. Sony Bravia 5 review: Price and release date The LG B6 delivers deep black tones and crisp textures (Image credit: Future) Release Date: July 2025 55-inch: $1,399.99 / £1,299 / AU$1,999 65-inch: $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 75-inch: $1,999.99 / £1,799 / AU$2,899 85-inch: $2,399.99 / £2,299 / AU$3,899 98-inch: $4,999.99 / £4,499 (around AU$8,570) While the Bravia 5 is affordable by Sony TV standards, $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 is no longer cheap for a 65-inch TV. The Bravia 5 retains much more of Sony’s mid-range — and even premium — TV DNA than expected based on similarly positioned models in previous Sony ranges, though. As a result, it has at least the potential to take a clear performance edge over more affordable rivals. Sony Bravia 5 review: Specs Screen type Backlight Master Drive VA mini-LED with local dimming Sizes available 55, 65, 75, 85 and 98 inches Refresh rate 120Hz Resolution 4K HDR support Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG Audio support 40W acoustic multi-audio speaker system featuring dual full-range (bass reflex) speakers and two ‘frame’ tweeters; Dolby Atmos and DTS:X decoding Smart TV Google TV (plus all main UK terrestrial broadcaster catch up apps for UK buyers) HDMI ports 4 (two full HDMI 2.1) Sony Bravia 5 review: Benchmark results Sony Bravia 5 review: Features (Image credit: Future) Mini-LED lighting Direct lighting with local dimming Bravia XR processor As I’ve hinted more than once already, the Sony Bravia 5 is packing much more feature heat than I would have expected it to, based on Sony TV ranges of the past. This is particularly true of the screen hardware at the Bravia 5’s heart. Designated one of Sony’s Master Backlight Drive panels, it is illuminated by mini-LEDs driven by a local dimming system that, according to my own counting efforts, operates across an impressive 240 zones. That’s 240 areas of the image that are capable of receiving their own light level, independent of their neighbors, according to the needs of the image. The Bravia 5’s panel is a VA type, too, which should further enhance contrast (though maybe not viewing angles). Meanwhile, even this far down Sony’s range, the brand's consistently impressive XR processor is still on hand to power all the constituent parts of the TV’s pictures. On top of this, rather than dropping down to 50/60Hz, the panel also maintains a native 120Hz refresh rate. Meanwhile, its support for high dynamic range images extends to Dolby Vision, as well as the more basic HDR10 and HLG formats. Sony is also unusual in the TV world for automatically applying an HDR upgrade to SDR sources on some of its picture presets. There’s no interest from Sony, though, in the HDR10+ format designed as an open-source alternative to Dolby Vision. The Bravia 5’s connections keep up with its step-up siblings. So you get four HDMIs (though only two support the TV’s full range of gaming features like VRR and ALLM), USB media playback support, and wireless support that includes Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.3, built-in Chromecast, Apple Airplay, and Apple HomeKit. (Image credit: Future) Sony’s TV business has long traded on its ‘from camera to TV’ product chain, and the potential for accuracy that this can bring. So as usual the Bravia 5’s Professional Mode setting, at least, will have been tuned alongside one of Sony’s professional mastering monitors, and the set is equipped with a bunch of so-called Calibrated modes designed to replicate as closely as possible the mastering standards of the Prime Video, Netflix and Sony Pictures Core video streaming services. Buying a Bravia 5 entitles you to 10 free films and 24 months of access to Sony Pictures Core too, by the way, complete with its unique high-bandwidth streaming speeds for enhanced picture quality. Further ‘third party’ endorsement finds the Bravia 5 earning an IMAX Enhanced badge, indicating that it has been deemed capable of doing justice to the special noise-limiting mastering processes and potential shifting aspect ratios associated with the IMAX Enhanced system. IMAX Enhanced titles are available on Sony Pictures Core and Disney+. The Bravia 5’s audio setup is pretty potent by mid-range TV standards. It offers two full range Bass Reflex-design drivers and two separated tweeters getting 10W a piece to deliver both Dolby Atmos and DTS:X soundtracks — the latter even includes the special tweaked version of DTS:X associated with IMAX Enhanced content. Features score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Picture quality Impressive brightness and light control Bold but also natural colour Genuine 4K sharpness and excellent 4K upscaling The Sony Bravia 5’s image quality instantly changes the fortunes of this level of Sony’s TV range, leaning much more towards the Sony TVs above it than those below. Particularly great to see is how much contrast the Bravia 5 retains for this level of Sony’s range. Black colors look deep and strikingly consistent, exhibiting minimal issues with backlight blooming around bright objects or general areas of clouding. That's despite the fact the screen is capable of hitting nearly 900 nit brightness peaks on a 10% HDR window and sustaining an OLED-beating 595 nits with a full 100% HDR window. Combining Sony’s backlight structure and XR Processor, the Bravia 5 can maintain more intensely bright highlights against dark backdrops than you’d expect for its price tag, despite how limited the clouding around such highlights is. This combination of bright stand-out objects and limited clouding is very difficult to achieve with locally dimmed TVs, yet the Bravia 5 makes it look easy. Dark scenes look stable, too, in the sense that you never feel aware of the sudden brightness jumps or obvious ‘handovers’ between different dimming zones as bright objects move around a dark backdrop. (Image credit: Future) Many screens with strong contrast performances are often capable of good color reproduction too — and this trend continues with the Bravia 5. In its Standard preset, it produces strikingly vibrant, rich and bold tones (actually upgraded to HDR if you’re watching an SDR source) that still feel balanced, full of subtlety and nuance, and connected to source tones for the most part. They feel more like amplifications of source content colors rather than aggressive departures from them. Unfortunately, the Bravia 5 pushes this amplification effect way too far in the Vivid preset, which is best avoided. But the Standard setting is an excellent bright room option, as well as actually being delicate and balanced enough to hold up as a dark room movie night option if your image tastes tend towards the bright and vibrant. Unlike most other TV brands, Sony doesn't offer a Filmmaker Mode preset for AV fans who favor ‘as the director intended’ viewing. Its Professional Mode, though, does pretty much the same thing, with an emphasis on trying to match the image as closely as possible to Sony’s professional video mastering monitor. Using Portrait Display’s Calman Ultimate software, G1 signal generator and C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, the accuracy of the Bravia 5 Professional mode was easy enough to demonstate. Errors recorded in both SDR and HDR across the board came in at well under the 3.0 DeltaE 2000 average beyond which errors might become visible to the human eye. (Image credit: Future) The Bravia 5’s Professional mode doesn’t just measure well. It also looks subjectively lovely, packed with the subtle texturing, immaculate color balance, and remarkable light control for a lower mid-range LCD TV. The benefits of Sony finally being able to introduce a superior core panel in a TV at the Bravia 5’s level are arguably at their most obvious in the Professional preset, in fact, given that this mode uses relatively few processing tools to help ‘boost’ its appearance. Inevitably, given it’s far from the most premium TV in Sony’s range, there are a few limitations to the Bravia 5’s picture performance. Dark scenes in the Professional mode look a little grayer than they do in Standard mode, and backlight blooming around bright objects can become more noticeable if you view the TV from an angle. Strangely, certain shades of red can look a bit over-ripe during dark scenes, and some dark shots also take on a slightly green undertone. Finally, some of Sony’s preset choices don’t actually help the Bravia 5’s pictures at all. Motion processing only really helps 24p movie sources if it’s switched to its True Cinema mode, for instance, with other settings tending to generate unwanted digital side effects or leave the image looking unnaturally smooth. I’d also recommend turning off the noise reduction features, especially with native 4K sources, to ensure the screen’s impressive native sharpness isn’t unnecessarily softened away. The Bravia 5’s issues are mild enough or easy enough to fix, though, that they don’t stop it from being an all-round excellent picture performer for its money. Picture quality score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Sound quality (Image credit: Future) Impressive clarity and detailing Sound doesn’t suffer with distortions Bass is a bit lightweight The Bravia 5’s sound joins its pictures in being impressively expressive and clean, working within the speaker’s limitations rather than pushing things beyond their breaking point as so many integrated TV sound systems are wont to do. Even the brightest, shrillest treble sounds are produced without sounding thin or brittle, while the mid-range is clean and pretty expansive, able to cope with the ebbs and flows of even quite dense action scenes without sounding forced, muddy or compressed. It uses its four-speaker system well to create a fairly large soundstage, too — one that’s well populated with accurately placed, crisp but never overstated details. My only complaint is that the Bravia 5 feels a bit light in the bass department. Dinosaur footprints, rumbling space ships, meaty explosions and the like don’t hit with quite as much heft as I’d like. At the same time, though, not even Hollywood’s most extreme bass moments cause the Bravia 5’s speakers to succumb to distracting crackles or distortions. Sound quality score: 4 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Design (Image credit: Future) Multi-point foot attachment Recycled plastic remote control Minimal frame The Bravia 5’s design doesn’t feel like much of a step-down at all from Sony’s Bravia 7 series. Its screen frame is extremely narrow, distracting scarcely at all from the pictures within, and it also stays fairly trim around the back for a lower mid-range LCD TV. Its feet look a little basic when attached to such an elegantly minimalistic screen, perhaps. But Sony has thoughtfully provided the option to attach them either quite close together or out towards the TV’s bottom corners, depending on the width of the furniture you want to stand the TV on. Build quality is good, too, and despite its relatively affordable position in Sony’s current TV range, it ships with two remote controls. The sleeker, more modern and more feature-rich handset is made largely made from recycled plastic, as part of Sony’s wide-ranging attempts to make the TV production process greener. Design score: 4 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Smart TV & menus LG's webOS 26 is easily one of the best smart TV platforms around (Image credit: Future) Google TV smart system YouView for full UK app coverage Optional Bravia Cam The Sony Bravia 5 runs the latest Google TV system very well, avoiding the sluggishness the system sometimes causes on less powerful TVs. Google TV carries pretty much all of the most popular and important video streaming services, and Sony has helpfully worked round Google TV’s blind spot when it comes to some of the UK’s most popular terrestrial broadcaster catch up services by adding the YouView app. Google TV can still feel a little overwhelming in its presentation and doesn’t feel as intelligent as some rival smart systems when it comes to recommending content based on your viewing habits. The smarter of the two remote controls Sony provides, though, makes navigation of the menus feel straightforward. On top of this, you can access a good range of features and issue quite complex search instructions just by talking to the Bravia 5 via the Google Assistant voice recognition system. You can even add basic gesture control features to the Bravia 5 if you cough up £200 for one of Sony’s Bravia Cam accessories. This add-on camera can also detect your location in the room and adjust the TV’s picture and sound settings accordingly, as well as issuing audio warnings if it detects anyone getting too close to the screen. I’m not personally convinced Bravia CAM does enough to justify its price, but if the features I’ve just described sound good to you, then fill your boots! Smart TV & menus score: 4.5 / 5 Sony Bravia 5 review: Gaming (Image credit: Future) 4K/120Hz support VRR support Perfect For PlayStation 5 support The Sony Bravia 5 is fairly, rather than brilliantly, well specified as a gaming display. For instance, while it does support 4K game feeds at 120Hz refresh rates, it only does so over two of its HDMIs, rather than all four. It also doesn’t stretch the refresh rate support to 144Hz or even 165Hz, like some rival TVs currently do. Similarly, while the Bravia 5 supports variable refresh rates, that support doesn’t extend to the AMD Freesync or Nvidia G-Sync systems. There is support for auto low latency mode switching, though, so the TV can automatically switch into its fastest responding picture mode when a game source is detected. While in this mode, the Bravia 5 takes just 13.3ms to render 60Hz gaming feeds. There’s support, too, for Sony’s unique Perfect For PlayStation 5 features, comprising a PS5-specific version of automatic game mode switching, and an excellent system where a connected PS5 is able to tell which Sony TV model it’s attached to, and automatically optimize its HDR output accordingly. You can also call up a dedicated gaming menu when the Bravia 5 is in Game mode, containing information on the game feed and a few helpful gaming assistants. Finally, the actual gaming experience when using one of the two wide-bandwidth HDMIs is very enjoyable. The TV’s vibrant, exceptionally sharp and contrast-rich pictures provide a perfect fit for today’s usually HDR and 4K graphics, while the rapid response time and VRR support means gaming never feels sluggish or laggy. Gaming score: 4 / 5 (Image credit: Future) Sony Bravia 5 review: Value Not so long ago, spending $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 to get a 65-inch TV as good and feature rich as the Sony Bravia 5 would have felt like a great deal. Recently, though, TCL in particular has drastically shifted the TV value ‘window’, with its bright, vibrant and gaming-friendly 65-inch C7K currently going for just £779. The Bravia 5 does offer more precision and balance in its pictures than the TCL C7K, but the price gap is big enough to mean you may feel like holding out for a special offer on Sony’s model, or searching beyond the most popular electronics retailers for a better deal. Value score: 3.5 / 5 Should I buy the Sony Bravia 5? Sony Bravia 5 scorecard Attributes Notes Rating Features Aside from a few gaming limitations, the Bravia 5 is well featured for its money. 4.5 / 5 Picture quality Vibrant, bright, sharp and contrast rich pictures reveal the presence of more excellent Sony backlighting and video processing systems. 4.5 / 5 Sound quality While bass heads might wish for a bit more low frequency impact, the Bravia 5’s sound is clean, punchy, detailed and unusually well staged. 4 / 5 Design With its choice of foot position, elegantly minimalist frame, slender frame and strong build quality, the Bravia 5 looks premium enough to match its price. 4 / 5 Smart TV and menus Google TV runs stably and reasonably slickly on the Bravia 5, making it easy to access the huge array of content options it offers. The set up menus are well organised and graphically rich, too. 4.5 / 5 Gaming Only two HDMIs support the Bravia 5’s full array of gaming features, and those features don’t include absolutely everything some rivals offer. However, the exclusive to Sony TVs Auto HDR ‘Perfect For PlayStation 5’ feature is excellent, and the screen feels responsive and immersive. 4 / 5 Value While the Bravia 5 is well priced for a Sony TV that performs as well as this one, competition at this price level is brutal these days. 3.5 / 5 Buy it if... You want that Sony picture feel for less The Bravia 5 holds on to more of the panel and processing prowess of more premium Sony TVs than you'd expect at this price. You have a PlayStation 5 The Bravia 5’s Perfect For PlayStation 5 features allow a PS5 console to automatically feed it optimized HDR games — a genuinely helpful feature given that HDR gaming is still in something of a ‘wild west’ stage at the moment. You want to put your TV on a narrow piece of furniture While the widest foot placement looks more elegant, Sony provides the option to place the Bravia 5’s feet close together as well. Don't buy it if... You are on a tight budget Some rivals, most notably TCL, sell bright, vibrant 65-inch TVs with good gaming features for substantially less than the Bravia 5 costs. You have more than two premium gaming sources Only two of the Bravia 5’s HDMI ports support the full range of cutting-edge gaming features that today’s gamers are looking for (4K/120Hz and VRR). You want a Filmmaker Mode and/or HDR10+ support If you happen to be a real fan of Filmmaker Mode presets and the HDR10+ rival to Dolby Vision HDR, you should know that the Bravia 5 doesn’t support either of these features. Sony Bravia 5 review: also consider Sony Bravia 5 TCL C7K LG C5 Samsung QN90F Price (65-inch) $1,499.99 / £1,499 / AU$2,299 $899.99 / £779 / AU$2,295 $1,399.99 / £1,599 / AU$2,699.99 $1,599.99 / £1,399 / AU$2,899 Screen type Backlight Master Drive VA mini-LED with local dimming Mini-LED with local dimming WRGB OLED Mini-LED with local dimming Refresh rate 120Hz 4K 144Hz (up to 288Hz at lower resolution) 144Hz 120Hz (up to 165Hz with Motion Xcelerator technology) HDR support HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG HDR10, HDR10+, HLG Smart TV Google TV (plus all main UK terrestrial broadcaster catch up apps for UK buyers) Google TV with YouView WebOS 25 Tizen OS HDMI ports 4 (two full HDMI 2.1) 4 (two HDMI 2.1) 4 x HDMI 2.1 4 x HDMI 2.1 TCL C7K With its extreme brightness, surprisingly good backlight control and uncompromising gaming features, the C7K has single-handedly rewritten the TV value rulebook. While Sony’s set delivers a more controlled image, the C7K’s bang for your buck is crazy. And it supports all four key HDR formats too. Read our full TCL C7K review . LG C5 With LG’s 2026 OLED TV range just arriving, at the time of writing you can buy 2025’s C5 at a knock down price. Every pixel in OLED TVs delivers its own color and light without compromising its neighbors, delivering stunning contrast. The C5 also delivers excellent gaming support, and some of the most accurate pictures around. Read our full LG C5 OLED TV review. Samsung QN90F Samsung’s flagship 4K mini-LED TV for 2025 is also still around as we wait for the brand’s 2026 models, and it looks like strong value at its current $1,599.99 / £1,399 / AU$2,899 price. Its impressive pictures are joined by four full HDMI 2.1 ports, and an Object Tracking Sound (OTS) system that does a strikingly good job of placing sound effects in the right place on screen. Read our full Samsung QN90F TV review. How I tested the Sony Bravia 5 Tested over three weeks Tested with 4K Blu-rays, multiple streaming platforms and resolutions, Freeview HD broadcasts, and HD Blu-rays Reviewed in both dark and light dedicated test room conditions, on its feet in both corner and mid wall positions I tested the Sony Bravia 5 over a three-week period in a variety of room conditions — including using it as a regular living room TV for more than a week. I checked out streamed content at a variety of resolutions from all of the main video streaming platforms, including Sony’s exclusive Sony Pictures Core high-bandwidth services. I also watched tuner channels and fed it a selection of our regularly used test Blu-rays and 4K Blu-ray discs. Gaming was explored using a PlayStation 5, an Xbox Series X and a gaming PC. Objective testing was performed using Portrait Displays’ Calman Ultimate analysis software, G1 signal generator, and C6 HDR5000 light meter. paragraphs: Recommended (Image credit: © Future) TechRadar Verdict With its Bravia 5 series, Sony has finally figured out how to take its premium TV talents mainstream. Picture performance is impressive overall, with bold color, strong contrast and minimal blooming, while its sound is detailed with plenty of presence. Its smart TV interface is flexible and easy to use and while it's lacking the odd gaming feature, its ‘Perfect For PlayStation 5’ feature goes some way to making up for this.

Jump To: Two-minute review Price & release date Specs Benchmark results Features Picture quality Sound quality Design Smart TV & menus Gaming Value Should you buy it? Also consider How we tested Sony Bravia 5: Two-minute review The Sony Bravia 5 is a mini-LED TV with crisp images, strong contrast and great gaming features. It occupies that level in Sony’s TV range where the brand has historically struggled to maintain its high standards. The Bravia 5, though, bucks this trend in pretty spectacular fashion.

The Sony Bravia 5 retains both mini-LED lighting and local dimming, for starters, as well as an 120Hz panel to keep gamers happy. Sony says the Bravia 5 LCD panels are still made to the brand’s Master Backlight Drive standard too, and they’re equipped with a full up-to-date version of the Google TV smart system.

There are ‘catches’ to this promising specification, of course. In particular, the Bravia 5 won’t benefit from as many dimming zones as the step up Bravia 7, or achieve so much brightness. In reality, though, the 65-inch Bravia 5 (AKA the K65XR55) delivers much less of a step down from Sony’s mid-range models than expected based on past Sony lines. Pictures are vibrant, crisp, full of contrast and just way less compromised than previous generations of the same level of Sony TV would have been.

articles.title_en: Đánh giá Sony Bravia 5: Khi công nghệ Mini-LED cao cấp trở nên dễ tiếp cận hơn
articles.dek_en: Dòng TV mới của Sony xóa nhòa khoảng cách với các model cao cấp nhờ bộ xử lý XR và hệ thống làm mờ cục bộ 240 vùng, dù vẫn còn một số hạn chế về cổng kết nối và độ sáng so với dòng Bravia 7.
articles.body_en:
What happened
Trong lịch sử, Sony thường gặp khó khăn trong việc duy trì tiêu chuẩn cao cấp trên các dòng TV phổ thông. Tuy nhiên, Bravia 5 (mã hiệu K65XR55 cho bản 65 inch) đã thay đổi định kiến này. Được định vị là dòng TV Mini-LED giá cả phải chăng nhất của hãng trong năm 2025, sản phẩm này kế thừa nhiều đặc tính kỹ thuật từ các dòng cao cấp để cạnh tranh trực tiếp trong thị trường TV 4K đang ngày càng khốc liệt.

Thay đổi kỹ thuật: Sức mạnh từ Master Backlight Drive và chip XR
Thay đổi cốt lõi nằm ở việc trang bị tấm nền VA Mini-LED với hệ thống điều khiển Master Backlight Drive, hỗ trợ làm mờ cục bộ (local dimming) trên khoảng 240 vùng độc lập. TV duy trì tần số quét thực 120Hz và được vận hành bởi bộ xử lý hình ảnh XR danh tiếng. Về âm thanh, hệ thống loa 40W Acoustic Multi-Audio bao gồm hai loa toàn dải và hai loa tweeter khung (frame tweeter) hỗ trợ cả Dolby Atmos và DTS:X.

The evidence so far
Trong thử nghiệm thực tế, Bravia 5 đạt độ sáng tối đa gần 900 nits (cửa sổ 10% HDR) và duy trì 595 nits trên toàn màn hình, vượt qua nhiều đối thủ OLED. Hình ảnh có độ tương phản sâu, hiện tượng hở sáng (blooming) được kiểm soát tốt. Đặc biệt, tính năng 'Perfect For PlayStation 5' giúp tự động tối ưu hóa HDR khi kết nối với máy game PS5, kết hợp với độ trễ đầu vào thấp chỉ 13. 3ms ở 60Hz mang lại trải nghiệm giải trí mượt mà.

Giới hạn và rủi ro: Sự đánh đổi về kết nối và độ sáng
Để có mức giá cạnh tranh, Bravia 5 bị cắt giảm số vùng làm mờ và độ sáng so với Bravia 7. Một hạn chế đáng tiếc là chỉ có 2 trong số 4 cổng HDMI hỗ trợ đầy đủ tính năng 2. 1 (4K/120Hz, VRR). Ngoài ra, góc nhìn của tấm nền VA còn hạn chế khi hiện tượng hở sáng dễ lộ diện nếu xem từ góc lệch. Sony cũng tiếp tục nói không với định dạng HDR10+ và không có chế độ Filmmaker Mode chuyên dụng.

What is still unclear
Dù có giá từ 1. 399 USD cho bản 55 inch, Bravia 5 vẫn cao hơn đáng kể so với các đối thủ như TCL C7K. Người dùng cần theo dõi các chương trình khuyến mãi để có mức giá tốt hơn. Ngoài ra, việc tích hợp sâu hệ sinh thái Google TV và các dịch vụ độc quyền như Sony Pictures Core (tặng 10 phim và 24 tháng streaming) sẽ là yếu tố then chốt để người dùng quyết định chi thêm tiền cho thương hiệu Nhật Bản thay vì các lựa chọn giá rẻ.

articles.title: Windows 11’s next security feature may cost you gaming performance
articles.hook: Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post .
articles.summary: Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post . Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post .

sections.heading: Where the sources line up
sections.body: Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs. Starting October 13th, 2026, all supported Windows 11 PCs will enable Memory Integrity by default. While Memory Integrity is primarily intended as a security feature, gamers may find it a hindrance.

sections.heading: Practical impact for readers
sections.body: What does it actually do? Well, Memory Integrity ensures that only verified kernel-mode code is loaded on the PC, blocking unsigned rootkits and raising the barrier to driver-based kernel attacks. The goal is for Windows 11 to be better protected against malware attacks.

sections.heading: Who should pay attention now

sections.heading: What is still unclear
sections.body: However, this feature has a major drawback: Memory Integrity can apparently slow down games. Tom’s Hardware measured years ago that HVCI combined with VBS (Virtualization-Based Security) causes games to run up to 15 percent slower. VBS is also enabled as part of this update, providing additional security features.

draft_context.source_title: Windows 11’s next security feature may cost you gaming performance
draft_context.description: Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post . Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs. Starting October 13th, 2026, all supported Windows 11 PCs will enable Memory Integrity by default. While Memory Integrity is primarily intended as a security feature, gamers may find it a hindrance. What does it actually do? Well, Memory Integrity ensures that only verified kernel-mode code is loaded on the PC, blocking unsigned rootkits and raising the barrier to driver-based kernel attacks. The goal is for Windows 11 to be better protected against malware attacks. Before Windows enables this feature, it will check eligible computers and verify whether the machine is ready for it. According to this support page , Memory Integrity requires the following hardware: 8th-generation Intel processor or newer AMD Zen 2 or newer Qualcomm Snapdragon 8180 or newer At least 8GB of RAM on x64 systems A 64GB SSD with firmware-enabled virtualization Drivers with confirmed compatibility with Memory Integrity However, this feature has a major drawback: Memory Integrity can apparently slow down games. Tom’s Hardware measured years ago that HVCI combined with VBS (Virtualization-Based Security) causes games to run up to 15 percent slower. VBS is also enabled as part of this update, providing additional security features. According to Tom’s Hardware , Microsoft confirmed in 2022 that “Memory Integrity and Virtual Machine Platform could affect gaming performance on some Windows 11 configurations, and advised gamers prioritizing performance that they could temporarily disable these protections while playing, warning that doing so reduces security.” Gaming performance losses are most likely to be noticeable on computers with older hardware. Tom’s Hardware continued, saying that Microsoft’s guidance for gamers recommended “temporarily disabling Memory Integrity and VMP where they interfere with gaming performance.”
paragraphs: Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post .

Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs. Starting October 13th, 2026, all supported Windows 11 PCs will enable Memory Integrity by default. While Memory Integrity is primarily intended as a security feature, gamers may find it a hindrance.

What does it actually do? Well, Memory Integrity ensures that only verified kernel-mode code is loaded on the PC, blocking unsigned rootkits and raising the barrier to driver-based kernel attacks. The goal is for Windows 11 to be better protected against malware attacks.

However, this feature has a major drawback: Memory Integrity can apparently slow down games. Tom’s Hardware measured years ago that HVCI combined with VBS (Virtualization-Based Security) causes games to run up to 15 percent slower. VBS is also enabled as part of this update, providing additional security features.

According to Tom’s Hardware , Microsoft confirmed in 2022 that “Memory Integrity and Virtual Machine Platform could affect gaming performance on some Windows 11 configurations, and advised gamers prioritizing performance that they could temporarily disable these protections while playing, warning that doing so reduces security.”
